title: AI Observability and Evaluation: Catch Silent LLM Failures
author: TechEniac Services LLP
summary: Your AI support assistant just told a customer they can get a 30-day refund. They're on the Free plan, and Free has no refunds. The API returned 200 OK in 1.2 seconds. There were no exceptions, CPU was normal, and the dashboard stayed green. Nothing in your monitoring knows anything went wrong. Your infrastructure is healthy. Your product is wrong. This is a silent failure : the system executes the request successfully but delivers the wrong outcome. Traditional monitoring asks whether the service is up, fast and error-free. AI applications need more questions answered: Did the model answer correctly? Was the answer supported by the retrieved documents? Did the agent call the right tool? Did a prompt change break something that used to work? Which step caused the bad answer? That takes two capabilities working together: evaluation and observability . What you'll build In this tutorial you'll build the loop that catches the refund bug above: A small evaluation dataset based on the refund scenario A Python evaluator that runs under pytest and in CI OpenTelemetry traces that show which step caused a bad answer A link between each failed evaluation and its trace ID A workflow that turns every production failure into a regression test All code runs against a deliberately flawed stub app, so you'll see a real failure first. Then swap in your own answer_question() . Prerequisites: Python 3.9+ and pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk pytest . 1. Monitoring, observability and evaluation aren't the same thing These terms get used interchangeably, but each answers a different question. Capability Question it answers Example Monitoring Is the system healthy? API error rate increased Observability What happened during this request? Retrieval returned an outdated document Evaluation Was the result right? The answer contradicted the approved policy Continuous evaluation Did a change make things worse? A new prompt fails previously passing cases In our refund example, monitoring says the model responded. Observability shows retrieval returned the Pro plan policy. Evaluation says that policy was wrong for a Free user. You need all three. OpenAI's evaluation best practices recommend task-specific success criteria, representative datasets, automated checks where possible, and human judgment. A trace becomes far more useful once it's connected to an evaluation result, which is what we'll do below. 2. The architecture: four components Before choosing a vendor or SDK, decide what you need to capture. A useful setup has four parts: Instrumentation records what happened: model calls, retrieval, tool calls, duration, token usage, errors. Observability backend stores traces and events so developers can investigate. Evaluation pipeline checks outputs against explicit requirements using deterministic assertions, reference answers, human reviewers or model-based judges. Feedback loop turns real failures into repeatable test cases that run against every future change. The piece most teams miss is the join between 2 and 3: every evaluation result should carry the trace_id of the request it judged. Without it, a failed test tells you that something broke, but not where . You can use OpenTelemetry for instrumentation, and a platform such as MLflow or LangSmith for tracing and evaluation workflows. You don't need all of them. Start with the smallest setup that gives you useful evidence. 3. Build an evaluation dataset before building dashboards A common mistake: read a handful of AI responses, decide they look fine, and ship. A few good examples tell you almost nothing about edge cases or regressions. Instead, build a small dataset where you know what acceptable behavior looks like. Create eval_cases.json : [ { "id" : "refund-free" , "question" : "Can I get a refund on the Free plan?" , "required_facts" : [ "no refunds" ], "prohibited_claims" : [ "30 days" , "30-day" ], "expected_behavior" : "answer" }, { "id" : "refund-pro" , "question" : "What is the refund window on the Pro plan?" , "required_facts" : [ "30 days" ], "prohibited_claims" : [ "no refunds" ], "expected_behavior" : "answer" }, { "id" : "refund-unknown-plan" , "question" : "What is the refund policy for the Enterprise Plus plan?" , "required_facts" : [], "prohibited_claims" : [ "30 days" , "no refunds" ], "expected_behavior" : "abstain" } ] These policies are illustrative. In a real project, required facts and prohibited claims should come from approved documentation and domain-expert review. Notice the two separate fields. required_facts is what a correct answer must contain. prohibited_claims is what it must never say. Defining both is better than comparing against one reference sentence, because many different answers can be correct. A solid dataset covers five categories: Normal cases: common requests. Boundary cases: incomplete, ambiguous or very long inputs. Negative cases: questions the available evidence can't answer. Adversarial cases: prompt injection, conflicting instructions, attempts to bypass access controls. Regression cases: failures you've already seen in production. Rare failures can be more damaging than common ones, so don't optimize only for the happy path. 4. Write your first automated evaluator Start with deterministic checks. They're cheap, repeatable, and ideal for rules you can state exactly. First, the flawed stub app. Save it as my_ai_app.py . Its retriever has a deliberate bug: it always returns the Pro plan policy, the way a real retriever might pick the wrong document. # my_ai_app.py (deliberately flawed stub) POLICIES = { ' free ' : ' The Free plan has no refunds. ' , ' pro ' : ' The Pro plan offers refunds within 30 days. ' , } def retrieve ( question ): # Bug: ignores the plan named in the question return [{ ' id ' : ' policy-pro-v2 ' , ' text ' : POLICIES [ ' pro ' ]}] def generate ( question , documents ): return documents [ 0 ][ ' text ' ] def answer_question ( question ): docs = retrieve ( question ) answer = generate ( question , docs ) return { ' answer ' : answer , ' abstained ' : False } Your real answer_question() should return the same structure: an answer string and an abstained boolean. Now the evaluator. Save it as evaluate.py : import json from pathlib import Path def load_cases (): return json . loads ( Path ( ' eval_cases.json ' ). read_text ( encoding = ' utf-8 ' )) def check ( case , result ): """ Return None if the case passes, otherwise a failure reason. """ answer = result . get ( ' answer ' , '' ) text = answer . casefold () if isinstance ( answer , str ) else '' # Prohibited claims fail every case, including abstentions for claim in case [ ' prohibited_claims ' ]: if claim . casefold () in text : return f ' prohibited claim present: { claim } ' if case [ ' expected_behavior ' ] == ' abstain ' : if result . get ( ' abstained ' ) is not True : return ' should have abstained ' return None missing = [ f for f in case [ ' required_facts ' ] if f . casefold () not in text ] return f ' missing facts: { missing } ' if missing else None def evaluate_case ( case , answer_question ): result = answer_question ( case [ ' question ' ]) reason = check ( case , result ) return { ' case_id ' : case [ ' id ' ], ' passed ' : reason is None , ' reason ' : reason } def run_evaluation ( answer_question ): results = [ evaluate_case ( c , answer_question ) for c in load_cases ()] failures = [ r for r in results if not r [ ' passed ' ]] passed = len ( results ) - len ( failures ) # Log IDs and reasons only, never raw user content for r in failures : print ( f " FAIL { r [ ' case_id ' ] } : { r [ ' reason ' ] } " ) print ( f ' { passed } / { len ( results ) } passed ' ) return { ' passed ' : passed , ' total ' : len ( results ), ' failures ' : failures } Add the regression test as test_quality_gate.py : from evaluate import run_evaluation from my_ai_app import answer_question def test_ai_quality_gate (): report = run_evaluation ( answer_question ) assert report [ ' total ' ] > 0 assert not report [ ' failures ' ] Run it: pytest -q Output (abridged): FAIL refund-free: missing facts: ['no refunds'] FAIL refund-unknown-plan: prohibited claim present: 30 days 1/3 passed There's the bug from the opening: a Free-plan user gets the Pro policy, and your green dashboard would never have shown it. Important limitation: substring matching isn't a general measure of factual correctness. A response can contain every required phrase and still mislead, and a correct paraphrase can fail a literal match. Use deterministic assertions for deterministic requirements, and add semantic or human evaluation where the task needs judgment. In a real project, keep the evaluation report as a CI artifact and avoid printing sensitive user content to build logs. 5. Know which metrics actually matter A single overall quality score can hide serious problems. Pick metrics based on the failure modes your application can't afford. Metric What it tells you Limitation Task success rate Whether the task was completed correctly Needs a reliable definition of success Groundedness Whether claims are supported by evidence The evidence itself can be wrong Retrieval precision and recall Whether the right documents were retrieved Doesn't prove the final answer is right Tool-call accuracy Whether the right tool and arguments were chosen A correct call can still fail to execute Abstention quality Whether unsupported questions are declined Both false refusals and unsafe answers matter p95/p99 latency How slow the slower requests get Says nothing about answer quality Cost per successful task What a correct outcome costs Depends on how you define success and cost Pass rate (passed cases divided by evaluated cases) is the simplest of these, and also the easiest to misread. A high pass rate on a small, easy dataset can coexist with frequent real-world failures, so always report dataset size, coverage and failure categories next to the number. Also evaluate at the right level. Failures happen at the single step (wrong tool), the full trace (retrieval plus generation), the conversation (lost context across turns), and the business outcome (the operation didn't actually succeed). A correct tool call is not a completed task, and a fluent answer is not a grounded one. 6. Add observability, and link it to your evaluations Evaluation tells you a test failed. Observability tells you why. Without a trace, you reproduce the request by hand and hope the failure happens again. With one, you can inspect each step: Step Evidence to capture Example failure Request Correlation ID, route, safe metadata Unexpected input format Retrieval Document IDs, relevance scores Outdated policy document Model call Model ID, prompt version, duration, tokens Changed prompt behavior Tool execution Tool name, validated arguments, status Wrong tool selected Validation Rule IDs and pass/fail Required fact missing Outcome Evaluation label, user feedback Wrong answer reached the user First, set up tracing. Save as tracing.py . This prints spans to the console so you can see them immediately; in production, swap the exporter for OTLP to your backend. from opentelemetry import trace from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import ConsoleSpanExporter , SimpleSpanProcessor provider = TracerProvider () provider . add_span_processor ( SimpleSpanProcessor ( ConsoleSpanExporter ())) trace . set_tracer_provider ( provider ) tracer = trace . get_tracer ( ' support-assistant ' ) Next, instrument the stub app. Replace answer_question in my_ai_app.py with: from tracing import tracer def answer_question ( question ): with tracer . start_as_current_span ( ' ai.request ' ): with tracer . start_as_current_span ( ' ai.retrieval ' ) as span : docs = retrieve ( question ) span . set_attribute ( ' app.retrieval.document_ids ' , [ d [ ' id ' ] for d in docs ]) with tracer . start_as_current_span ( ' ai.generation ' ) as span : span . set_attribute ( ' gen_ai.request.model ' , ' stub-model ' ) answer = generate ( question , docs ) return { ' answer ' : answer , ' abstained ' : False } The gen_ai.* attribute follows OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions ; app.* is a custom name. The conventions are still evolving, so check the current specification and your instrumentation library before depending on a specific attribute. The example deliberately records document IDs rather than raw prompts or document text. Now the join. Update evaluate_case in evaluate.py so each result carries the trace ID: from tracing import tracer def evaluate_case ( case , answer_question ): with tracer . start_as_current_span ( ' eval.case ' ) as span : span . set_attribute ( ' eval.case_id ' , case [ ' id ' ]) result = answer_question ( case [ ' question ' ]) reason = check ( case , result ) span . set_attribute ( ' eval.passed ' , reason is None ) trace_id = format ( span . get_span_context (). trace_id , ' 032x ' ) return { ' case_id ' : case [ ' id ' ], ' passed ' : reason is None , ' reason ' : reason , ' trace_id ' : trace_id , } And print it in the failure line: print(f"FAIL {r['case_id']}: {r['reason']} (trace {r['trace_id']})") . Because answer_question runs inside the eval.case span, its retrieval and generation spans share the same trace ID. Paste that ID into your trace backend and you'll see ai.retrieval returned policy-pro-v2 for a Free-plan question. You've gone from "test failed" to "retrieval ignored the plan" in one step. Don't stop at the final response An agent can retrieve the wrong documents, retry a failed tool, fall back to a second model, and still return a plausible answer. If you record only the final response, that history is gone. For multi-step applications, trace the whole workflow, use consistent correlation IDs, and make sure asynchronous work preserves trace context. For more, see OpenTelemetry's GenAI observability walkthrough . 7. Use model-based judges carefully Some requirements can't be checked with string matching: Is the answer relevant? Does it contradict the supplied documents? Is it complete enough to solve the user's problem? An LLM judge can score outputs against an explicit rubric. Provider-agnostic sketch (pass in your own call_llm ): import json JUDGE_PROMPT = """ You are grading a support answer. Question: {question} Allowed evidence: {evidence} Answer: {answer} Return only JSON: {{ " grounded " : bool, " relevant " : bool, " complete " : bool, " failure_reason " : str}} """ def judge ( question , answer , evidence , call_llm ): raw = call_llm ( JUDGE_PROMPT . format ( question = question , answer = answer , evidence = evidence )) return json . loads ( raw ) A judge is itself a model. It can miss errors, favor verbose answers, or agree with a fluent but wrong one. Add safeguards: Write rubrics with examples of passing and failing outputs. Validate judge decisions against human-reviewed examples. Use deterministic checks wherever a requirement can be checked exactly. Track disagreement between the judge and human reviewers. Recalibrate when models, prompts or criteria change. Never rely on a single judge score for high-impact decisions. Save human review for the decisions where a wrong answer is expensive. 8. Turn production failures into regression tests Here's a scenario that's easy to picture. A SaaS company's support assistant starts telling Free-plan users they can claim a refund. Support tickets don't spike, because the answer sounds reasonable and most people just accept it. A few weeks later, finance notices a pile of refund requests that don't match the policy. Someone finally pulls the trace for one of the bad answers. The generation step looks fine; the model summarized exactly what it was given. The retrieval step is the problem: it returned the Pro plan policy, because a recent re-indexing job had dropped the plan metadata the retriever filtered on. Every Free-plan refund question was quietly matching the Pro document. Nothing in the logs flagged it, and no test covered it. The fix was a few lines in the indexer. The more useful change came after: the team added that question to the evaluation dataset as a regression case, so the next change to indexing or retrieval would fail in CI instead of reaching a customer. After a failure like that, the loop is always the same: Retrieve the failed trace by its correlation ID. Find the earliest step where behavior diverged from expectations. Redact sensitive information before turning it into a reusable example. Add the case to the evaluation dataset. Fix the underlying cause. Run the full regression suite and compare against the previous baseline. Monitor the deployment for similar failures. Different failures need different responses: Failure Likely next step Retrieval returned irrelevant documents Inspect queries, filters and ranking Correct evidence, incorrect answer Inspect prompt, model output and eval cases Correct answer, wrong tool action Fix authorization, tool schemas or execution logic Sudden latency increase Inspect spans, queue time, model duration and retries Higher cost per successful task Inspect token usage, retries and model routing Quality regressed after deployment Compare eval results and trace distributions across versions Fix the failure at its source. Adding another sentence to the prompt every time something goes wrong is not a fix. 9. Add an evaluation gate to CI/CD Run your dataset whenever you change anything that can affect behavior: system prompts, model versions and parameters, retrieval and embedding models, document ingestion and chunking, tool schemas, and safety validators. A minimal GitHub Actions workflow: name : ai-eval on : [ pull_request ] jobs : eval : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - uses : actions/setup-python@v5 with : python-version : ' 3.11' - run : pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk pytest - run : pytest -q The pipeline order is: code or prompt change, then unit tests, then the golden evaluation dataset, then a baseline comparison. Critical regressions fail the build. Otherwise review quality and cost trade-offs, deploy gradually, monitor traces, and feed reviewed failures back into the dataset. Don't use an arbitrary universal pass-rate threshold. A regression in a formatting task and a regression in financial actions or access control deserve different release policies. A sensible starting policy: No failures in mandatory deterministic security tests. No unacceptable regression in critical task-success metrics. Quality compared against a known baseline. Latency and cost within limits for the service. Human approval for changes to high-impact workflows. A fixed test set also goes stale. Keep expanding it with production failures and reviewed feedback. 10. Privacy: observability can create a second data leak AI traces can contain user messages, personal data, proprietary documents and API arguments. OpenTelemetry's own conventions warn that some GenAI attributes may hold sensitive information. Before enabling content capture, ask: Do we need the full prompt or response, or are document IDs and redacted excerpts enough? Who can access production traces, and for how long are they retained? Are secrets and personal data removed before export? Are tenant boundaries enforced in the backend itself? Can users request deletion where applicable? Default to metadata-only traces, and enable content capture narrowly for specific debugging workflows. Redact before data reaches the exporter, restrict access, and encrypt in transit and at rest. Also, a system prompt is not a security boundary. Your application and tools must enforce authorization, not rely on the model choosing to follow instructions. 11. What to implement first You don't need an AI platform on day one. Follow this order: Phase 1: Baseline. Define success for your main workflow. Build a small reviewed dataset covering normal, boundary, negative and adversarial cases. Add deterministic checks. Phase 2: Instrument. Trace retrieval, model calls, tools and validation. Capture duration, errors, token usage and safe correlation metadata. Phase 3: Connect. Attach trace IDs to evaluation results, record failure categories instead of only a score, and turn reviewed failures into regression tests. Phase 4: Automate. Run evals in CI, compare against a baseline, add sampled online evaluation where cost and latency allow, and feed production failures back into the dataset. Phase 5: Harden. Add privacy controls, retention policies, alert thresholds and release criteria. Track quality next to latency, reliability and cost. Order matters. Instrumenting everything before you know what you need to learn produces telemetry without improving your ability to diagnose failures. Conclusion Monitoring only tells you the service responded. To know whether the answer was right you need evaluation, and to know why it was wrong you need traces. Without both, that Free-plan customer keeps hearing about 30-day refunds. You don't need a platform to start. Pick one workflow, write 20 cases you can defend, trace retrieval and generation, and add the eval to CI. Every real failure after that becomes a permanent test. You won't prevent every bad answer. What you can do is catch the next one before a customer does, see why it happened, and make sure it only happens once. Need help shipping reliable AI features? title: A Telegram bot for restocks and price drops: JSON-LD first, CSS selectors as a fallback
author: DevKit
summary: Written with AI assistance; the template itself was built and tested by the author's AI assistant. You want a ping when a sold-out item comes back, or when a price falls by a meaningful amount. You don't need a scraping farm for that. Most shops already publish the data you need in a machine-readable form, and a small asyncio process with SQLite can watch a few dozen product pages. This article walks through the design of a bot built as a reusable template (Python, aiogram 3, httpx, selectolax, SQLite). Every idea below can be reimplemented in an afternoon without buying anything. Step 1: read structured data before touching CSS Most shops emit schema.org Product markup in a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag, because search engines want it. That's far more stable than a CSS class that changes with each redesign. So the first adapter just looks for it. JSON-LD shows up in a few shapes: a single object, a list, or an object with @graph . A small generator flattens them: import json def iter_json_ld_blocks ( html_parser ): for node in html_parser . css ( ' script[type= " application/ld+json " ] ' ): raw = node . text ( deep = True ) if not raw or not raw . strip (): continue try : data = json . loads ( raw ) except json . JSONDecodeError : continue if isinstance ( data , list ): yield from data elif isinstance ( data , dict ): if isinstance ( data . get ( " @graph " ), list ): yield from data [ " @graph " ] else : yield data Broken JSON in one block is skipped rather than fatal, since real pages often carry several blocks from different plugins. Offers, availability and variants Availability is a URL such as https://schema.org/InStock . Take the last path segment, normalise it, and map it to three states: in stock, out of stock, unknown. AVAILABILITY_MAP = { " instock " : " in_stock " , " limitedavailability " : " in_stock " , " preorder " : " in_stock " , " backorder " : " out_of_stock " , " outofstock " : " out_of_stock " , " soldout " : " out_of_stock " , " discontinued " : " out_of_stock " , } def normalize_availability ( raw ): if not raw : return " unknown " key = raw . rsplit ( " / " , 1 )[ - 1 ]. strip (). lower () key = key . replace ( " " , "" ). replace ( " _ " , "" ). replace ( " - " , "" ) return AVAILABILITY_MAP . get ( key , " unknown " ) (The real map has a few more entries such as OnlineOnly , InStoreOnly and PreSale . Whether a pre-order counts as "in stock" is a judgment call, so change it if you disagree.) The "unknown" state matters. If a page says nothing clear, you don't want to alert on it. Some ProductGroup pages, commonly Shopify themes, carry no top-level offer. Price and availability sit on each variant under hasVariant . The adapter handles this in the simplest possible way: offer = first_offer ( node . get ( " offers " )) or {} if not offer and isinstance ( node . get ( " hasVariant " ), list ) and node [ " hasVariant " ]: first_variant = node [ " hasVariant " ][ 0 ] if isinstance ( first_variant , dict ): offer = first_offer ( first_variant . get ( " offers " )) or {} price = parse_price ( offer . get ( " price " ) or offer . get ( " lowPrice " )) currency = offer . get ( " priceCurrency " ) Be aware of the limitation: it reads the first variant only. If you care about one specific size or colour, point the bot at that variant's own URL, or extend this to match on SKU. If no Product JSON-LD exists, the adapter also tries OpenGraph tags ( product:price:amount , product:availability ) before giving up with a parse error. Prices need cleaning too, since "1 234,56" and "1,234.56" both occur. The JSON-LD adapter strips non-numeric characters and treats a lone comma as a decimal separator. It is a heuristic, so test it on your own sites. Step 2: CSS selectors for sites without markup Some storefronts, usually hand-built ones, have no structured data. For those, you declare selectors once per site in a YAML file, matched by a glob on the URL: sites : - name : example-generic-shop url_pattern : " https://shop.example.com/product/*" adapter : generic_css interval_seconds : 1800 jitter_seconds : 300 selectors : name : " h1.product-title" price : " span.price" availability : " div.stock-status" in_stock_text : " in stock" out_of_stock_text : " sold out" The adapter extracts the text of each selector. Availability is a case-insensitive substring check, with your configured phrases tested first and a few common English and Russian phrases as defaults: def detect_availability ( text , in_stock_text , out_of_stock_text ): if text is None : return " unknown " lowered = text . lower () if out_of_stock_text and out_of_stock_text in lowered : return " out_of_stock " if in_stock_text and in_stock_text in lowered : return " in_stock " if any ( p in lowered for p in ( " in stock " , " available " )): return " in_stock " if any ( p in lowered for p in ( " out of stock " , " sold out " , " unavailable " )): return " out_of_stock " return " unknown " Note the order: "out of stock" is checked before the generic "in stock" patterns would match, which avoids the classic bug where "not available" reads as available. Keep your own out_of_stock_text specific for the same reason. If none of your selectors match, the adapter raises a parse error that tells you to check the YAML, so a redesigned page fails loudly instead of silently reporting nothing. Step 3: change detection that alerts once The trick for "alert once" is boring: persist the last known state per product, compare the new reading to it, then overwrite it. The comparison itself is a pure function with no I/O, which makes it easy to unit test. def detect_changes ( old_price , old_available , new_price , new_availability , threshold_percent ): events = [] new_available = new_availability == " in_stock " if old_available is not None and new_availability != " unknown " : if not old_available and new_available : events . append ( " back_in_stock " ) elif old_available and not new_available : events . append ( " out_of_stock " ) if old_price and new_price is not None and new_price != old_price : change = abs ( new_price - old_price ) / old_price * 100 if change >= threshold_percent : events . append ( " price_change " ) return events (The real function returns ChangeEvent dataclasses carrying the URL, name and old/new price, but the logic is the same.) Details worth copying: old_available is None means this is the first check. There is no baseline, so no event. You won't get a flood when you add a product. An unknown reading never triggers anything. The price threshold is a percentage (default 5.0 , set with PRICE_CHANGE_THRESHOLD_PERCENT ), and it fires on rises as well as drops. The message text says which direction. After each check, the new state is written back in SQLite, plus a row in a price_history table: await conn . execute ( " UPDATE products SET name = COALESCE(?, name), last_price = ?, " " last_currency = ?, last_available = ?, last_checked_at = ? WHERE id = ? " , ( name , price , currency , None if available is None else int ( available ), now , product_id ), ) await conn . execute ( " INSERT INTO price_history (product_id, price, available, checked_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?) " , ( product_id , price , None if available is None else int ( available ), now ), ) await conn . commit () Because the baseline moves forward on every check, a back-in-stock alert fires once per transition. A caveat I'd rather you hear from me: a slow drift, say 2% per day, never crosses a 5% threshold between two consecutive checks, so it never alerts. If that matters, compare against the price from your last alert , not the last check. Another quirk: if one check returns unknown , the stored availability becomes null, so the next definite reading is treated as a new baseline and does not alert. Step 4: Telegram alerts Subscriptions live in SQLite ( users , products , subscriptions ), so one product can have several subscribers and gets fetched once. Sending is a loop around aiogram's send_message , and one blocked user must not stop the rest: async def send_events ( bot , events , subscriber_tg_ids ): for event in events : text = event . format_message () for tg_id in subscriber_tg_ids : try : await bot . send_message ( tg_id , text ) except TelegramAPIError as exc : logger . warning ( " failed to notify %s: %s " , tg_id , exc ) Users add products with /add <url> , which also runs a first check. /list , /remove <id> and /check cover the rest. Bot replies and alerts come from a small strings table with English and Russian versions, picked by a LANGUAGE=en|ru setting. Step 5: scheduling and polite fetching A single asyncio loop wakes every 30 seconds and asks the database which products are due: never checked, or older than their interval plus a random jitter. The defaults are 1800 s interval and up to 300 s jitter. Jitter keeps products from becoming due in lock-step. threshold = interval + ( random . uniform ( 0 , jitter_seconds ) if jitter_seconds else 0 ) if ( now - last ). total_seconds () >= threshold : due . append ( product ) The fetcher adds the following, all configurable through environment variables: a robots.txt check per host, cached, enabled by default ( RESPECT_ROBOTS_TXT ); a disallowed URL raises an error instead of being fetched. If robots.txt is missing or can't be fetched, the fetcher assumes allowed; a per-host limit, default 6 requests per minute; up to 3 attempts with linear backoff (2 s, then 4 s) on HTTP errors; a 15 s timeout. A failed fetch or parse is logged and skipped; the loop carries on. Step 6: JS-rendered prices (optional) If the price is injected by JavaScript, the HTML contains nothing to parse. The template includes a small Playwright fetcher that loads the page in Chromium and returns the rendered HTML: async with async_playwright () as p : browser = await p . chromium . launch () try : page = await browser . new_page ( user_agent = user_agent ) await page . goto ( url , timeout = 20_000 , wait_until = " networkidle " ) return await page . content () finally : await browser . close () Playwright is imported lazily, so it isn't required unless you use it. It is switched on with USE_PLAYWRIGHT=true or per site with playwright: true in sites.yaml . Browser fetches wait on the same per-host rate limiter as plain HTTP requests, and if Playwright is enabled but not installed the bot logs one error and falls back to httpx. Retries and the robots.txt check apply only to the plain HTTP path. Also check whether the site offers a JSON endpoint behind that JavaScript first; it's lighter and kinder to the server. Step 7: run it With Docker Compose, the SQLite file lives in a named volume so subscriptions survive restarts: services : stockbot : build : . image : stockbot:latest restart : unless-stopped env_file : - .env volumes : - stockbot-data:/app/data volumes : stockbot-data : Without Docker, a systemd unit does the job: [Service] Type = simple User = stockbot WorkingDirectory = /opt/stockbot EnvironmentFile = /opt/stockbot/.env ExecStart = /opt/stockbot/.venv/bin/python -m stockbot Restart = on-failure RestartSec = 5 NoNewPrivileges = true PrivateTmp = true The bot needs a token from BotFather in BOT_TOKEN and refuses to start without it. Being a good citizen Monitoring a page is still automated traffic to someone else's server. Read each site's terms of service and robots.txt before adding it. The template honours robots.txt by default, but a permissive robots file is not the same as permission in the terms. Keep intervals modest. Half an hour is the default here; for most restocks, hourly or slower is plenty. Don't lower it just because you can. Watch a handful of products, not a whole catalogue. If a store has an official API, a product feed or an email "notify me" button, use that instead of scraping. If a site asks you to stop or starts returning errors, back off. What this is not Not a scalping or checkout bot. It reads public product pages and sends you a message. It doesn't log in, fill carts or buy anything. Not an anti-bot toolkit. It does not solve CAPTCHAs, spoof fingerprints or defeat bot protection. For transparency about what it does contain: it rotates the User-Agent from a configurable list, and the fetcher accepts an optional proxy list, which is empty by default. If a site blocks you, treat that as a "no" and don't work around it. One process, one SQLite file. There is no queue, no worker pool and no horizontal scaling. That's fine for personal or small-shop use, and not designed for thousands of URLs. Heuristic parsing. Price formats, variant handling and availability wording vary by site, so test each one before trusting it. Get the template The ideas above are enough to build your own. If you'd rather start from working code, the full template (source, 56 tests, Dockerfile and Compose file, systemd unit, README in English and Russian) is sold for 9 USDT through the Telegram shop . There is also a free monitoring kit for a single VPS .

title: Fixing the Extra-Ingredient Problem in MiniChefGPT: Which Model Should We Use?
author: Marie Claire NIYOMUGENGA
summary: In our NLP course we built MiniChefGPT, a small GPT-style model that turns a list of ingredients into a recipe title and steps. It works, but it has one clear flaw: it uses ingredients nobody gave it. This post looks at models and techniques that could fix that, and explains which one I would choose and why. The project in numbers A decoder-only Transformer with 3 blocks, 4 attention heads, 128-dimensional embeddings and a 256-token context. A byte-level BPE tokenizer with a 4,096-token vocabulary. 1,053,440 parameters, trained from scratch on a CPU within a 30-minute budget. 9,979 cleaned Food.com recipes, split into 8,983 for training, 502 for validation and 494 for testing. Test perplexity of 16.68. My part of the team project was the residual connections around the attention and feed-forward blocks. The problem We gave the app four ingredients: chicken, garlic, onion and tomato. It returned a recipe titled "chicken soup" whose steps use broccoli, rice, chicken broth and noodles. None of those were requested, and tomato was never used. Our own notebook check agrees. On four custom ingredient lists, the generated recipes mention 56% of the requested ingredients on average. On 12 held-out ingredient lists the figure is 27%. Why it happens A tiny model with little data. One million parameters trained from scratch on about 9,000 recipes learn how recipes sound. They do not learn a rule like "use only these ingredients". Noisy training data. Our notebook notes that the source recipes sometimes mention ingredients that are missing from their own ingredient list. The model learns that extra ingredients are normal. No rule against extras when generating. We rank several candidate recipes by how many requested ingredients they mention, but nothing penalises ingredients that were not requested. How we should measure the fix Our coverage score only counts requested ingredients that appear. It cannot see extras. I would add an extra-ingredient rate : the share of food words in the generated recipe that are not in the input list, allowing a few pantry staples such as salt, pepper, water and oil. A good fix raises coverage and lowers this rate on the same held-out lists. Candidate models and techniques Option What it is Does it help with extras? Catch Constrained decoding Rules applied while generating, such as bad_words_ids to ban tokens and prefix_allowed_tokens_fn to allow only some Yes, directly: banned food words cannot appear Needs a food word list. Forcing words with constrained beam search needs do_sample=False Chef Transformer (T5) A T5 text-to-text model trained on RecipeNLG, a dataset of 2,231,142 recipes, with an ingredient list as input Maybe: far more data than our 10,000 recipes Different data and architecture, so it is hard to compare with our model, and it can still add ingredients Small pretrained decoder with LoRA Start from SmolLM2 (135M, 360M or 1.7B parameters) or Qwen3 (0.6B or 1.7B), both Apache 2.0, and fine-tune on our recipes Likely: it already knows language, and Instruct versions are trained to follow instructions Not guaranteed. Needs a GPU, but the free Colab T4 is enough Retrieval with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 A 22.7M-parameter embedding model that turns text into 384 numbers, used to find real recipes with similar ingredients Yes, real recipes are consistent The app copies existing recipes instead of creating new ones Ingredient checker A model that finds food words in the output, for example an NER model trained on TASTEset (700 recipes, more than 13,000 labelled entities) Catches extras after generation It checks but does not generate, and a simple word list built from our data may do the same job My choice: SmolLM2-360M-Instruct, fine-tuned with LoRA I would replace our from-scratch model with SmolLM2-360M-Instruct , fine-tuned on our recipes with LoRA. LoRA trains small adapter matrices instead of every weight, so training is light. My reasons: Same design, much more knowledge. It is a decoder-only Transformer like MiniChefGPT, so our pipeline of ingredients in and recipe out barely changes. It has about 340 times more parameters (360 million against 1.05 million) and is already pretrained, so it starts with language knowledge instead of learning from 9,979 recipes alone. It can follow an instruction. We can write the task as "use only these ingredients", which our scratch model cannot understand. It is cheap to run. In fp16, 360 million parameters take about 0.7 GB (parameters times 2 bytes), which fits easily on a free Colab T4 with 16 GB. The licence is Apache 2.0 , so there is no gate or paid API. Why not the others? Chef Transformer uses a different dataset and architecture, which makes it hard to compare with our results. Qwen3-1.7B is probably stronger, but it is almost five times bigger and has a thinking mode to switch off, so I would keep it as a stretch goal. Retrieval gives consistent recipes but copies them. Constrained decoding and an ingredient checker are not alternative models, so I would add them on top of my choice. I have not run this yet. A bigger model can still invent ingredients, so I would not claim success until the extra-ingredient rate drops on held-out lists. First experiment Turn recipe_10000.csv into instruction examples such as "Use only these ingredients: chicken, garlic, onion, tomato. Write a title and steps." Fine-tune SmolLM2-360M-Instruct with LoRA on the same training split, and keep our validation and test splits so results stay comparable. Generate with a banned-word list (sketch below, not tested). Compare coverage and extra-ingredient rate on the same 12 held-out lists and 4 custom tests. # Food words seen in the training recipes (ingredient names only) food_words = { w for r in train_rows for ing in r [ " ingredients " ] for w in ing . split ()} # Words the user gave, plus pantry staples we allow allowed = { w for ing in user_ingredients for w in ing . split ()} | { " salt " , " pepper " , " water " , " oil " } # Ban every other food word while generating banned = [ tok ( " " + w , add_special_tokens = False ). input_ids for w in food_words - allowed ] out = model . generate ( ** inputs , bad_words_ids = banned , do_sample = True , temperature = 0.7 , top_p = 0.9 , max_new_tokens = 200 ) This sketch ignores plural forms and capital letters, so a real version needs word variants. What I took away A bigger model is only part of the answer. The extra ingredients come from the data, the model size and the decoding, and each one needs its own fix. Measuring extras, not only coverage, is what tells us whether a change really helped. title: Reconcile Logs, Tool Calls, and Diffs Before You Trust a Trace
author: Sam Sun
summary: An agent trace is not one record. It is three records that never fully agree: the log line, the tool call, and the diff. The log says what the program believed was happening. The tool record says what the runtime actually dispatched. The diff says what the filesystem finally accepted. When those three disagree, you get a bug class that no single source can show you. A green log with a red diff is an unlogged write. A dispatched call with an empty diff is a lie about work done. A log that announces a retry the runtime never issued is an incident note that will mislead the next reader. Reconcile the three before you read anything else in the trace. The fixture first, because a harness you cannot reproduce is a rumor Start with a trace you can hand to a colleague. This one has a clean read, a clean write, and two planted disagreements. { "run_id" : "r-42" , "logs" : [ { "t" : 0.00 , "msg" : "plan ready" }, { "t" : 0.40 , "msg" : "tool read_file start" }, { "t" : 0.90 , "msg" : "tool read_file ok" }, { "t" : 1.20 , "msg" : "retrying write_file" } ], "tool_calls" : [ { "name" : "read_file" , "start" : 0.40 , "end" : 0.90 , "args" : { "path" : "src/app.py" }}, { "name" : "write_file" , "start" : 1.10 , "end" : 1.60 , "args" : { "path" : "src/app.py" }} ], "diffs" : [ { "path" : "src/app.py" , "added" : 4 , "removed" : 0 }, { "path" : "tests/test_app.py" , "added" : 2 , "removed" : 1 } ] } Read it as a reviewer and you already feel the friction. Something edited a test file that no tool call claims to have touched. Something said "retrying" while only one write exists. The point of the harness is to make that friction mechanical, so a nightly job catches it instead of a tired human at 11pm. A harness small enough to audit The join is plain set arithmetic plus one regex, and it returns a list rather than printing as it goes, which keeps it testable. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ reconcile.py - join logs, tool calls, and diffs into one finding list. """ import json import re import sys MUTATING = { " write_file " , " edit_file " , " delete_file " , " apply_patch " } BLOCKING = { " silent_write " , " phantom_call " } def reconcile ( trace ): findings = [] calls = [ c for c in trace [ " tool_calls " ] if c [ " name " ] in MUTATING ] written = { c [ " args " ]. get ( " path " ): c for c in calls } diff_paths = { d [ " path " ]: d for d in trace [ " diffs " ]} for path , d in diff_paths . items (): if path not in written : findings . append ({ " kind " : " silent_write " , " path " : path , " detail " : f ' + { d [ " added " ] } /- { d [ " removed " ] } , no mutating call ' }) for path , c in written . items (): if path not in diff_paths : findings . append ({ " kind " : " phantom_call " , " path " : path , " detail " : f ' { c [ " name " ] } dispatched, nothing changed ' }) for line in trace [ " logs " ]: m = re . search ( r " retry\w*\s+(\w+) " , line [ " msg " ]) if not m : continue name = m . group ( 1 ) seen = sum ( 1 for c in trace [ " tool_calls " ] if c [ " name " ] == name ) if seen < 2 : findings . append ({ " kind " : " retry_unrecorded " , " path " : name , " detail " : f ' log@ { line [ " t " ] : . 2 f } claims retry of { name } ; { seen } call recorded ' }) return findings def main ( path ): findings = reconcile ( json . load ( open ( path ))) for f in findings : print ( f ' { f [ " kind " ] : < 16 } { f [ " path " ] : < 20 } { f [ " detail " ] } ' ) blocking = [ f for f in findings if f [ " kind " ] in BLOCKING ] print ( f ' { len ( findings ) } findings ( { len ( blocking ) } blocking) ' ) return 1 if blocking else 0 if __name__ == " __main__ " : sys . exit ( main ( sys . argv [ 1 ])) Run it against the fixture and the disagreements surface in a fixed order, which matters if you plan to diff the output between runs. $ python reconcile.py trace.json silent_write tests/test_app.py +2/-1, no mutating call retry_unrecorded write_file log@1.20 claims retry of write_file ; 1 call recorded 2 findings ( 1 blocking ) $ echo $? 1 The exit code is the contract. Advisory findings (an unexplained retry) return 0 and inform. Blocking findings (a mutation nobody dispatched) return 1 and stop the pipeline. That split is the whole design: you want the retry note in the report, and you want the silent write to fail the run. Four disagreements worth naming Kind Shape of the evidence Blocking silent_write Diff path with no mutating call Yes phantom_call Mutating call with no diff at its declared path Yes retry_unrecorded Log claims a retry the call list cannot confirm No redirect_suspect Exactly one unexplained write and one unexplained call, paired by order Review The last row is a heuristic and should stay labelled as one. Pairing a lone orphan call with a lone orphan diff is a reasonable guess, not proof. Keep it advisory until you have seen it be right on your own traces. What this cannot see Read-only tools are exempt by the MUTATING set, so a shell tool that mutates files through sed -i will produce a false silent_write . Path normalization bites too: symlinks, absolute versus relative paths, and case differences all break the join. Concurrent runs sharing a working tree will interleave diffs and produce findings that are artifacts of scheduling rather than agent behavior. In-memory state, network side effects, and anything that never touches the working tree are simply outside the model. The harness answers one narrow question — do these three records describe the same run — and it answers it only as well as your tool registry is honest. The fixture test comes next, because a harness with no test is just another opinion. Ten lines of pytest pinning the exact finding set is enough. from reconcile import reconcile import json def test_fixture_findings (): trace = json . load ( open ( " trace.json " )) kinds = {( f [ " kind " ], f [ " path " ]) for f in reconcile ( trace )} assert kinds == {( " silent_write " , " tests/test_app.py " ), ( " retry_unrecorded " , " write_file " )} Running it where the traces already land A reconciliation step earns its keep as a scheduled job, not a manual script. Once a night, over yesterday's traces, writing findings to disk and letting the exit code drive a notification is the smallest useful version. I run that nightly job on the free server option of MonkeyCode rather than on a laptop, so the harness sits next to the trace store instead of depending on someone remembering to run it. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Free-tier terms and limits change, so check the project's own page for the current offer rather than trusting any number quoted in a blog post. Free model access is a good fit for exactly one narrow job here: mapping tool names from different SDKs ( str_replace_editor , apply_patch , write ) onto your MUTATING taxonomy. That mapping is boring, it breaks whenever you add an integration, and it must never be trusted blindly. Sketch, not production code: # pseudocode: model proposes a mapping, the frozen fixture verifies it proposed = classify_tool_names ( unmapped_names ) # model call assert proposed == FROZEN_EXPECTED # test gate TAXONOMY . update ( proposed if proposed else RULE_MAP ) # rule map fallback The rule map is the default. The model fills gaps between releases, and the frozen fixture decides whether the answer ships. If the assertion fails, you fall back and read the diff — which is the same discipline the harness itself is built on. Who should skip this Single-turn scripts with no file mutations will produce empty finding lists forever. Teams already capturing full OpenTelemetry spans plus a diff-per-tool-call record have solved this at the source, and a reconciliation pass on top is redundant ceremony. And if your traces are large enough that a nightly Python pass over them is the expensive part, fix retention first — reconciliation over a sampled week usually tells you everything a full month would. If you keep a trace store and have no reconciliation step, run this against your last twenty runs before you change any prompt. The disagreements you find tend to be older than your current bug.

title: A publish gate for AI-assisted posts: check every claim before it goes out
author: Todd Doane
summary: If an AI agent drafts what you publish, the risk is not bad grammar. It is a confident number nobody measured, a feature that does not exist, or a paragraph of stock phrases with your name on it. We let our store's daily agent post under a real person's name, so we built a gate it cannot skip. What goes wrong without one A language model writes what is plausible. Plausible is fine for a first draft and wrong for a public claim. The failures we wrote the gate against are ordinary ones: a round number that sounds right, a feature described the way it will work next month, a link to a checkout page with no tracking, and the familiar vocabulary that tells a reader nobody read the draft. Asking the agent to "be accurate" does not fix this. The agent that wrote the claim is the one judging it, in the same context, with the same blind spots. The check has to sit outside the writing step and it has to be able to say no. The gate, in three layers A facts file is the only source of truth Every claim and every number a post may use lives in facts.md , each with its evidence: a file path, a command and its output, or a URL. If it is not in the file, it is not claimable. The file also has a "not claimable" section: customer counts, benchmarks, anything nobody has measured. Writing that section down is what keeps later posts honest. Deterministic checks are the floor Numbers: every number in the body must appear in facts.md , or the line carries a source link. Years, times, versions and list numbering are exempt. Phrases: a built-in list of stock AI phrases plus your own "Banned phrases" list from voice.md . Structure: no emoji, at most one exclamation mark, no rhetorical-question openers, a cap on em-dash density. Links: every link must resolve, and checkout links must carry utm_source so you can see which post sent the buyer. These cost nothing to run and they never get tired. They catch the cheap mistakes before a model is involved. An LLM checks each claim, and fails closed The last check sends the draft and the facts file to a model and asks for a verdict per claim: SUPPORTED, UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED. Anything other than SUPPORTED fails the post. If the model cannot be reached, the gate fails too. A check that passes when it cannot run is not a check. A PASS writes a small sidecar file with the SHA-256 of the post body. Every publisher script calls one function before it posts: side = require_verified ( path , body ) # refuses if the sidecar is missing, # the hash differs, or the LLM step was skipped Edit one word after the PASS and the publisher refuses until the gate runs again. That rule stops an agent from tweaking a post after it passed. It does not stop an agent with write access from changing the publisher itself; that part is still code review. What it caught, and what it did not The gate checks content. Today it showed us the edge of that. Our Show HN post passed the gate, the publisher submitted it and printed PUBLISHED, and the account's submissions page was empty. Hacker News had answered with a notice that it is temporarily restricting Show HNs from new accounts. The publisher had trusted the redirect after submitting and, when it could not find the item, reported a generic URL as success. That is a publisher bug, not a content problem, and we handled it the way we handle any failure: find the cause, fix it, add the test, then recover. The publisher now reports success only when the item appears under the account's own submissions, saves HN's response page otherwise, and reports the restriction as declined. We did not retitle the post to get around the rule; the draft is parked and the rule is logged. A gate tells you a post matches your facts file and your voice guide. It cannot tell you a community will take it, and your publishers need their own proof that the post actually exists. Try the pattern without buying anything Start with the cheapest part: a facts.md with evidence per line and a "not claimable" section, plus a rule in your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md that nothing is published unless every number in it is in that file. Then add the hash lock: write the body's hash on approval and refuse to publish if it changed. Those two steps are the core of the pattern. The free Agent Ops Kit Lite (MIT) has the CLAUDE.md structure this runs inside. Disclosure: I sell the finished version. Publish Gate v1 is verify_post.py with configurable facts and voice files, any model CLI through PUBLISH_GATE_LLM (default claude -p ), the require_verified helper, an example dev.to publisher, templates, a directive for your agent and 8 tests: $19, or $29 bundled with the Agent Ops Kit, at calyx-ai.net . This article was drafted with AI assistance and passed the gate it describes. Originally published at calyx-ai.net .

title: React Native vs React.js: Key Differences, Examples, and When to Use Each
author: Ansh Sheladiya
summary:
React Native vs React.js is a common question for developers deciding how to build modern applications. Both technologies use React's component-based architecture, JavaScript, and declarative UI principles, but they target different platforms and solve different problems. React.js is primarily used to build interactive web applications that run in browsers, while React Native helps developers build native mobile applications for Android and iOS. Understanding their differences can help you choose the right technology for your project, team, and long-term maintenance strategy. In this guide, we will compare their rendering approaches, components, styling, performance considerations, development workflows, and practical use cases. We will also explore a runnable JavaScript example that demonstrates how both approaches can share application logic while using platform-specific interfaces. React Native vs React.js: Architecture, Differences, and Practical Examples 1. What Is React.js? React.js is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, primarily for websites and web applications. It allows developers to create reusable components, manage state, respond to user interactions, and efficiently update the browser interface when application data changes. React components commonly render HTML elements such as div , button , and input . Styling is typically handled through CSS, CSS modules, utility frameworks, or CSS-in-JS libraries, while routing can be implemented with libraries such as React Router. 2. What Is React Native? React Native is a framework for building native mobile applications using React and JavaScript. Instead of rendering browser HTML elements, it uses components such as View , Text , Pressable , and TextInput to create mobile interfaces through the platform's native rendering infrastructure. React Native supports Android and iOS, with additional platform capabilities available through its ecosystem. Developers can reuse business logic and many application components across platforms, although certain features require platform-specific implementations or native modules. 3. Key Differences Between React Native and React.js Rendering: React.js renders interfaces in a browser using the DOM, while React Native renders mobile interfaces using native platform components. This distinction affects component selection, styling, accessibility, and integration with device capabilities. Styling: React.js commonly uses CSS and browser styling features. React Native uses JavaScript style objects with properties inspired by CSS, but its styling system does not support every browser CSS feature and has its own layout behavior. Navigation: Web applications generally use URL-based routing and browser navigation. Mobile applications commonly use stack navigation, tab navigation, or other mobile navigation patterns, often implemented with libraries such as React Navigation. Platform capabilities: React.js can access browser APIs, subject to browser permissions and security restrictions. React Native can integrate with mobile features such as cameras, notifications, location services, and native device APIs through supported APIs and libraries. Performance: Performance depends on implementation, rendering work, network requests, and the application's architecture. React.js performance is influenced by browser rendering and JavaScript execution, while React Native performance also depends on native rendering, JavaScript work, and communication with platform capabilities. 4. Can You Share Code Between React.js and React Native? Yes. Both technologies can share business logic, data validation, API clients, authentication helpers, utility functions, and many state-management patterns. However, browser-specific elements and mobile-specific UI components generally need separate implementations. For example, an order total calculation does not depend on whether the interface runs in a browser or a mobile application. The interface displaying that total does depend on the platform: React.js might use a div , while React Native would use View and Text . 5. Practical JavaScript Example The following example demonstrates a platform-independent shopping cart calculation. It uses ordinary JavaScript functions to calculate subtotals, discounts, and final prices, then prints the results with step-by-step console messages. This example runs directly in Node.js or a browser console because it does not depend on React or React Native packages. In a real application, the shared functions could live in a common module imported by separate React.js and React Native interfaces. 6. When Should You Choose Each Technology? Choose React.js when you need a website, dashboard, admin panel, e-commerce storefront, content platform, or browser-based SaaS application. It is particularly suitable when search engine visibility, URLs, responsive layouts, and integration with browser capabilities are important requirements. Choose React Native when you need Android and iOS applications with mobile-oriented navigation, device integrations, and platform-specific user experiences. It can reduce duplicated application logic across mobile platforms, but it does not eliminate all native development or platform-specific work. If your product needs both a website and mobile apps, using React.js and React Native together can be a practical strategy. Sharing domain logic and API contracts while maintaining separate platform-specific interfaces often provides a good balance between reuse and user experience. /* * React Native vs React.js * Shared business logic demonstration * * Run with: node react-comparison.js * * This file uses plain JavaScript so the same calculation * logic can be reused by web and mobile applications. */ // Step 1: Define reusable product data. const products = [ { id : 1 , name : " Wireless Mouse " , price : 799 , quantity : 2 }, { id : 2 , name : " Mechanical Keyboard " , price : 2499 , quantity : 1 }, { id : 3 , name : " USB-C Cable " , price : 299 , quantity : 3 } ]; console . log ( " Step 1: Product data loaded. " ); console . log ( `Number of products: ${ products . length } ` ); // Step 2: Calculate the subtotal without modifying the input. function calculateSubtotal ( items ) { return items . reduce (( total , item ) => { return total + item . price * item . quantity ; }, 0 ); } console . log ( " 
 Step 2: Calculating subtotal... " ); const subtotal = calculateSubtotal ( products ); console . log ( `Subtotal: ₹ ${ subtotal . toFixed ( 2 )} ` ); // Step 3: Calculate a percentage discount. function calculateDiscount ( amount , percentage ) { if ( amount < 0 || percentage < 0 || percentage > 100 ) { throw new RangeError ( " Invalid amount or discount percentage. " ); } return amount * ( percentage / 100 ); } console . log ( " 
 Step 3: Applying a 10% discount... " ); const discountPercentage = 10 ; const discount = calculateDiscount ( subtotal , discountPercentage ); console . log ( `Discount: ₹ ${ discount . toFixed ( 2 )} ` ); // Step 4: Calculate shipping using a reusable business rule. function calculateShipping ( amount ) { // Example policy: shipping is free for orders of ₹2,000 or more. return amount >= 2000 ? 0 : 99 ; } console . log ( " 
 Step 4: Calculating shipping... " ); const discountedSubtotal = subtotal - discount ; const shipping = calculateShipping ( discountedSubtotal ); console . log ( `Shipping: ₹ ${ shipping . toFixed ( 2 )} ` ); // Step 5: Produce a complete order summary. function createOrderSummary ( items , discountRate ) { const orderSubtotal = calculateSubtotal ( items ); const orderDiscount = calculateDiscount ( orderSubtotal , discountRate ); const amountAfterDiscount = orderSubtotal - orderDiscount ; const orderShipping = calculateShipping ( amountAfterDiscount ); return { itemCount : items . reduce (( count , item ) => count + item . quantity , 0 ), subtotal : orderSubtotal , discount : orderDiscount , shipping : orderShipping , total : amountAfterDiscount + orderShipping }; } console . log ( " 
 Step 5: Building the final order summary... " ); const summary = createOrderSummary ( products , discountPercentage ); // Step 6: Format the data for display on any platform. function formatCurrency ( amount ) { return `₹ ${ amount . toFixed ( 2 )} ` ; } console . log ( " 
 Step 6: Order summary " ); console . log ( " ------------------------------ " ); console . log ( `Total items: ${ summary . itemCount } ` ); console . log ( `Subtotal: ${ formatCurrency ( summary . subtotal )} ` ); console . log ( `Discount: ${ formatCurrency ( summary . discount )} ` ); console . log ( `Shipping: ${ formatCurrency ( summary . shipping )} ` ); console . log ( `Final total: ${ formatCurrency ( summary . total )} ` ); console . log ( " ------------------------------ " ); // Step 7: Demonstrate a simple validation check. function validateProducts ( items ) { return items . every (( item ) => { return ( Number . isFinite ( item . price ) && item . price >= 0 && Number . isInteger ( item . quantity ) && item . quantity > 0 ); }); } console . log ( " 
 Step 7: Validating cart data... " ); console . log ( `Cart is valid: ${ validateProducts ( products )} ` ); // Step 8: Export functions when this file is used as a CommonJS module. // A React.js or React Native project can import shared logic // from an appropriate module in its own application architecture. if ( typeof module !== " undefined " && module . exports ) { module . exports = { calculateSubtotal , calculateDiscount , calculateShipping , createOrderSummary , formatCurrency , validateProducts }; } console . log ( " 
 Example completed successfully. " ); Conclusion React Native and React.js share the same React philosophy, but they serve different application platforms. React.js is primarily designed for browser-based experiences, while React Native focuses on building mobile applications with native platform integration. The most important architectural decision is to separate reusable business logic from platform-specific user interfaces. This makes it easier to maintain consistent calculations, validation rules, and data handling without forcing web and mobile applications to share components that were designed for different environments. For JavaScript developers, learning React.js first can establish a strong foundation in components, props, state, hooks, and application architecture. Moving to React Native then becomes easier because many concepts remain familiar, even though styling, navigation, platform APIs, and release workflows differ. Ultimately, choose the technology that best fits your users and product requirements rather than treating one as universally better. title: I built HandFonty: turn your handwriting into an installable font in your browser

The reference letters are drawing guides; they are never included in your exported font. This is a hands-on lettering tool: the characters come from your strokes. Once you type a sentence, uneven spacing can become much more noticeable than the shape of an individual glyph. HandFonty lets you adjust the space before and after each character, its vertical position and scale, and the global letter spacing. Neighbouring letters stay visible while you make changes, so you can judge the rhythm of the text. There are also glyph variants and custom ligatures in the Pro feature set, for lettering that needs more than one version of a character or a custom combination of letters. 3. Preview and export an actual font Preview a pangram or type your own text, then build and download OTF and TTF files. These are vector fonts that can be installed on macOS and Windows and used in design tools. One deliberate choice: missing characters are never silently replaced with letters from another font. title: Testing Failure Paths in Fintech Onboarding: A Practical Engineering Checklist
author: Strikeloan
summary: Financial onboarding flows are easy to test when everything works. A user submits valid information, an API returns success, and the application moves to the next screen. Real systems are less predictable. A network request may time out after the server has processed it. A third-party verification service may become unavailable. A user may tap Submit twice, refresh a page, or leave halfway through an application. In financial applications, these situations can create duplicate records, confusing statuses, privacy issues, and unnecessary support requests. Testing the happy path is necessary, but it is not sufficient. Here is a practical approach to testing failure paths in fintech onboarding workflows. 1. Start with a workflow state model Before writing tests, identify the valid states of the workflow. For example, a simplified onboarding process might use these states: draft submitted verification_pending verification_failed eligible_for_review rejected completed These are illustrative application states, not a universal financial-industry standard. Define which transitions are permitted. A draft might become submitted, but a completed application should not silently return to draft because a delayed response arrived. Representing the workflow explicitly helps prevent invalid transitions from being scattered across controllers, frontend components, and background jobs. A transition test should verify both the expected state change and the transitions that must be rejected. 2. Test timeouts separately from failures A timeout does not always mean an operation failed. Consider a client submitting an application: The client sends a request. The server validates and stores the application. The server sends a response. The connection fails before the client receives it. The client sees a timeout, but the server may already have completed the operation. If the client blindly retries, the system could create duplicate applications. Test at least three distinct scenarios: The request never reaches the server. The server rejects the request before committing changes. The server commits the operation, but the response is lost. The third case is especially important because it tests whether the application can recover from uncertainty without repeating the underlying action. 3. Make retry behavior explicit Retries are useful for temporary failures, but they should not be automatic for every error. A reasonable policy distinguishes between transient failures and permanent failures. A temporary network issue might justify a bounded retry with backoff. Invalid input generally requires correction rather than repetition. For operations that must not be duplicated, consider an idempotency key or another server-side deduplication mechanism. A robust implementation should define: How the client identifies a logical operation How the server recognizes a repeated request How long the idempotency record remains valid What happens if the same key is reused with a different payload How concurrent duplicate requests are handled The exact implementation depends on the architecture and operation. An idempotency key is not a substitute for database constraints or transaction design. 4. Simulate third-party service failures Financial onboarding often depends on external systems for identity verification, document processing, eligibility checks, or other services. Do not test only the successful response from each dependency. Use mocks, controlled test doubles, or a sandbox environment to simulate: Connection timeouts HTTP 5xx responses Rate limiting Malformed responses Unexpected response delays Authentication failures Partial or inconclusive results The application should distinguish between a definitive business outcome and a technical failure. For example, a verification service being unavailable should not automatically be interpreted as a failed identity check. The workflow may need to remain pending until the result can be retrieved or retried safely. 5. Verify privacy in error handling and logs Errors are another failure path that deserves dedicated tests. A raw exception may contain request payloads, document references, authentication details, or other sensitive information. Logging the entire request can expose information that operators do not need. Prefer structured logs containing operational context such as: A correlation ID The workflow stage A sanitized error category The dependency involved The retry count The final outcome Avoid logging secrets or unnecessary personal information. Where identifiers are required for debugging, use appropriate access controls, retention limits, and privacy-preserving identifiers. Add automated tests that deliberately trigger errors and inspect captured logs for prohibited fields. It is not enough to verify that the application returns a generic error message to the user; sensitive information must also be absent from logs and telemetry. 6. Test concurrent requests and stale responses Concurrency bugs often escape ordinary functional testing. Two requests may attempt to update the same application. A background job may finish after a user has cancelled the workflow. A delayed response may overwrite a newer state. Useful tests include: Submitting the same operation concurrently Updating an application while a verification job is running Delivering the same webhook more than once Delivering events out of order Retrying a job after a worker crash Depending on the system, protection may require optimistic locking, database transactions, unique constraints, version numbers, or idempotent event processing. The objective is to ensure that the final state is valid regardless of the order in which requests and events arrive. 7. Turn the checklist into automated tests A test suite should cover more than individual API responses. It should verify the end-to-end invariants of the workflow. Here is a compact checklist: Test scenario Expected invariant Client times out after server commit No duplicate logical operation Dependency returns a temporary error Workflow remains recoverable Verification result is inconclusive No unsupported final decision Duplicate webhook arrives Event is not applied twice Two updates race Invalid state transitions are prevented Application fails validation No unintended partial commit An exception contains sensitive fields Sensitive data is not logged A background worker retries Processing remains safe and bounded Run these tests at the appropriate level: unit tests for state transitions, integration tests for persistence and transaction behavior, and end-to-end tests for the complete workflow. Where possible, inject failures deterministically rather than depending on random network instability. Deterministic tests are easier to reproduce and debug. Final thoughts Reliable financial workflows are defined not only by what happens when every dependency succeeds, but also by what happens when the system is uncertain. A good failure-path test suite asks four questions: Can the operation be repeated safely? Can the workflow recover without inventing a business outcome? Can concurrent events leave the system in an invalid state? Can the system explain the failure without exposing sensitive information? Answering these questions early can make financial applications easier to maintain, safer to operate, and less confusing for users. Disclosure: This article was drafted with assistance from AI. The author should verify the technical details, adapt the examples to their own engineering experience, and take responsibility for the published content.

title: OpenAI moves frontier model training offline: what it means for agent training
author: Tadna
summary: OpenAI says it will no longer give its frontier models live internet access while they are being trained.
